Density of the Rationals

See that every interval, however narrow, hides a rational. Bigger denominators make the ticks denser.

Between any two numbers sits a fraction. Narrower gaps need bigger denominators. Chop the scale finely enough and some tick lands in every gap. The same trick works around irrationals.

For example, keep cutting a 🍰 cake in half, again and again. The pieces shrink without end. Pick any thin gap, and a thinner piece exists. That piece is the fraction landing inside.

Show proof

  1. Problem 2 alone gives only one rational, so apply it twice: with the midpoint m=(x+y)/2m = (x + y)/2m=(x+y)/2, applying problem 2 in (x,m)(x, m)(x,m) gives a rational rrr with x<r<mx < r < mx<r<m, and applying it in (m,y)(m, y)(m,y) gives a rational sss with m<s<ym < s < ym<s<y; since r<m<sr < m < sr<m<s, there are rationals r<sr < sr<s inside (x,y)(x, y)(x,y).

    Put z=r+(s−r)22z = r + (s - r)\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z=r+(s−r)22​​.

    Since 1<2<41 < 2 < 41<2<4 and squaring is strictly increasing on [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞) (problem 1 of the sqrt2-irrational scene, plus the n-th root scene), 1<2<21 < \sqrt{2} < 21<2​<2 — hence 0<22<10 < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} < 10<22​​<1.

  2. Since s−r>0s - r > 0s−r>0, 0<(s−r)22<s−r0 < (s-r)\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} < s - r0<(s−r)22​​<s−r; adding rrr gives r<z<sr < z < sr<z<s. With x<rx < rx<r and s<ys < ys<y, x<z<yx < z < yx<z<y — zzz lies in the interval.

  3. Now zzz is irrational: if it were rational, 2=2(z−r)s−r\sqrt{2} = \frac{2(z - r)}{s - r}2​=s−r2(z−r)​ would be rational too (the right side is arithmetic on rationals with nonzero denominator) — contradicting Proposition 4.4.4 that 2\sqrt{2}2​ is irrational (problem 1 of the sqrt2-irrational scene). Hence zzz is irrational with x<z<yx < z < yx<z<y.

  4. Corollary: every open interval of the real line contains both rationals and irrationals. Density of the rationals does not mean "almost all" reals are rational — quite the opposite is true (the countability scene).
